title: When “Proficient” Doesn’t Equal Educated
author: Educated and Free
summary: A veteran public school teacher argues that parents cannot trust the proficiency bands on annual state tests, because each state sets its own cut scores and several have lowered them, producing an honesty gap against the NAEP benchmark. Since NAEP never reports an individual child's score, the author proposes that parents diagnose their own children directly. He recommends two short reading checks, a nonsense word test for phonemes and a grade-level reading passage test, and points parents to free phonics tools for any gaps. He also offers AI-assisted mastery tests tied to the Common Core literacy and math standards plus a section on E.D. Hirsch style cultural literacy. Parents are told to administer the tests across short sessions without hinting, score each skill 0 to 2, and treat low scores as information rather than a learning disability diagnosis. The piece frames this as a way of giving mom and dad better information than schools, which have incentives to move every child along, are willing to provide.
points: State proficiency labels are set by state-chosen cut scores, so a rise or fall in the share of proficient students can reflect a political decision rather than learning, as the Oklahoma reversal shows.
NAEP is the trustworthy benchmark but is never reported for an individual child, which leaves parents without a reliable external measure of where their own child stands.
The suggested home diagnostic starts with phonemes and grade-level reading because decoding gaps are the cheapest for a parent to fix directly.
The scoring rule of 2 for independent success, 1 for success after a prompt, and 0 for failure even with support gives parents a simple record of what a child has and has not learned.
Hirsch-style cultural literacy is treated as part of what a child should know, so the author adds a content-knowledge section covering science, history and literature.
quotes: American education feels broken because schools face incentives that push toward grade inflation and social promotion, even of students far behind in basic measures of competence.
K-12 bureaucrats, usually with some teachers thrown in to make the process look legitimate set the number that means a child is “proficient”.

The problem with NAEP is that you don’t ever get to review your child’s individual score. At best, a district’s scores will be published, but not necessarily your child’s school and certainly not your individual son or daughter.
If your child struggles on this test, this is where you, mom and dad, can get HUGE bang for the buck by stepping into the breach and directly teaching phonemes to your child.

Parents, being the primary custodians of their children’s long-term well-being, need much better information about where their child stands academically and benefit from the identification of specific gaps in their child’s education.
Avoid the urge to help; don’t teach, hint or correct while your child works. Your goal is to get a clear idea of how much your child has learned.

Your child is almost certainly fine, but your local school may not be. It’s better to know your child’s areas of weakness and address them now rather than hope someone in the school building will recognize and correct them before they cause larger downstream effects.
